Hi Marcelo, Nora here. Quick one. The tour tomorrow is still on, nine o'clock at the harbor. Weather? Looks fine, I think. Rain later, maybe, but I hope not. You said you could not make out half of what the guide said last time. Neither could the Germans, so do not worry. He has a broad accent, and he rattles off the names of every island in about five seconds. My advice? Do not try to catch every word. Get the gist, fill in the gaps, and ask me after. Oh, and the boat engine is loud, so the background noise will drown out a lot of it anyway. Coffee before? Let me know. See you tomorrow.

Why is native English so hard to follow, even when you know every word? Three reasons. First, natives say less than you expect. They drop words. Coming? means are you coming. Sounds good means that sounds good. And they answer with tiny pieces. I think so. I hope not. So do I. If you are waiting for a full sentence, the moment has already gone. Second, the important words are loud, and the small ones almost disappear. People slur them together, or say them under their breath. Third, there is always background noise. A cafe, a car, a boat. So stop trying to hear every word. Listen for the stressed words, get the gist, and let your brain fill in the gaps. That is exactly what native speakers do with each other, every single day.

First, Nora sends a quick voice message: the tour is still on, at nine o'clock at the harbor. Then Marcelo boards the boat and sits at the back, where the engine is loudest. After that, the guide rattles off the names of the islands, and Marcelo zones out after the third one. Next, he tunes in again when the story of the shipwreck begins, and gets the gist. Finally, he tells Nora what he understood, and she says he understands far more than he thinks.
